Tree Diagram Lie Algebras of Differential Operators

and Evolution Partial Differential Equations11 1 2000 Mathematical Subject Classification. Primary 17B30, 35F15, 35G15; Secondary 35C15, 35Q58

Xiaoping Xu22 2 Research Supported by China NSF 10431040

Institute of mathematics, Academy of Mathematics & System Sciences

Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100080, P. R. China

Abstract

A tree diagram is a tree with positive integral weight on each edge, which is a notion generalized from the Dynkin diagrams of finite-dimensional simple Lie algebras. We introduce two nilpotent Lie algebras and their extended solvable Lie algebras associated with each tree diagram. The solvable tree diagram Lie algebras turn out to be complete Lie algebras of maximal rank analogous to the Borel subalgebras of finite-dimensional simple Lie algebras. Their abelian ideals are completely determined. Using a high-order Campbell-Hausdorff formula and certain abelian ideals of the tree diagram Lie algebras, we solve the initial value problem of first-order evolution partial differential equations associated with nilpotent tree diagram Lie algebras and high-order evolution partial differential equations, including heat conduction type equations related to generalized Tricomi operators associated with trees.

1 Introduction

In 1905, Schur [Si] proved that the maximum number of linearly independent commuting n×nn\times n matrices is [|n2/4|]+1[|n^{2}/4|]+1. Jacobson [J1] (1944) gave a simplified derivation of Schur’s result. Malcev [M] (1945) determined the abelian subalgebras of maximal dimension of a finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra. Kostant [K1] (1965) found a connection of Malcev’s result with the maximal eigenvalue of the Laplacian acting on the exterior algebra of the Lie algebra via the adjoint representation. Moreover, he [K2] (1998) related abelian ideals of a Borel subalgebra to the discrete series representations of the Lie group. Panyushev and Röhrle [PR] (2001) described spherical orbits in terms of abelian ideals. Furthermore, Panyushev [P] (2003) gave a correspondence of maximal abelian ideals of a Borel subalgebra to long positive roots. Suter [Sr] (2004) determined the maximal dimension among abelian subalgebras of a finite-dimensional simple Lie algebra purely in terms of certain invariants and gave a uniform explanation for Panyushev’s result. Besides, he gave a generalization and explanation of the symmetry property of a certain subposet of Young’s lattice. Kostant [K3] (2004) showed that the powers of the Euler product and abelian ideals of a Borel subalgebra are intimately related. There were many results on non-abelian ideals of Borel subalgebras ( cf. [AKOP], [CP1-CP4], [KOP]) and structure of nilpotent Lie algebras (e.g., cf. [FS], [GK], [Sl1], [Sl2]).

Barros-Neto and Gel’fand [BG1,BG2] (1998,2002) studied fundamental solutions for the Tricomi operator. Our initial motivation of this work is to solve heat conduction type evolution partial differential equation related to generalized Tricomi operators associated with trees. It turns out that some abelian ideals of certain “tree diagram solvable Lie algebras” have to be used. This motivates us to introduce two nilpotent Lie algebras and their extended solvable Lie algebras associated with a general tree diagram. Familiar examples of such solvable Lie algebras are the Borel subalgebras of special linear Lie algebras and symplectic Lie algebras. The abelian ideals of these solvable Lie algebras are completely determined. Moreover, we completely solve the first-order evolution partial differential equations associated with nilpotent tree diagram Lie algebras and high-order evolution partial differential equations, including heat conduction type equations related to generalized Tricomi operators associated with trees. Below we give a more detailed technical introduction.

Barros-Neto and Gel’fand [BG1,BG2] (1998, 2002) studied solutions of the equation

ux​x+x​uy​y=δ⁡(x−x0,y−y0)u_{xx}+xu_{yy}=\delta(x-x_{0},y-y_{0}) (1.1)

related to the Tricomi operator ∂x2+x∂y2\partial_{x}^{2}+x\partial_{y}^{2}. A natural generalization of the Tricomi operator is ∂x12+x1∂x22+⋯+xn−1∂xn2\partial_{x_{1}}^{2}+x_{1}\partial_{x_{2}}^{2}+\cdots+x_{n-1}\partial_{x_{n}}^{2}. The equation

ut=∂x12(u)+∂x22(u)+⋯+∂xn2(u)u_{t}=\partial_{x_{1}}^{2}(u)+\partial_{x_{2}}^{2}(u)+\cdots+\partial_{x_{n}}^{2}(u) (1.2)

is a well known classical heat conduction equation related to the Laplacian operator ∂x12+∂x22+⋯+∂xn2\partial_{x_{1}}^{2}+\partial_{x_{2}}^{2}+\cdots+\partial_{x_{n}}^{2}. As pointed out in [BG1, BG2], the Tricomi operator is an analogue of the Laplacian operator. An immediate analogue of heat conduction equation is

ut=∂x12(u)+x1​∂x22(u)+⋯+xn−1​∂xn2(u).u_{t}=\partial_{x_{1}}^{2}(u)+x_{1}\partial_{x_{2}}^{2}(u)+\cdots+x_{n-1}\partial_{x_{n}}^{2}(u). (1.3)

Naturally, we should also consider similar equations related to the graph:

which is the Dynkin diagram of the orthogonal Lie algebra s​o​(2​n,ℂ)so(2n,\mathbb{C}) when n1=n2=1n_{1}=n_{2}=1, and the Dynkin diagram of the simple Lie algebra of types E6,E7,E8E_{6},\;E_{7},\;E_{8} if (n0,n1,n2)=(3,1,2),(3,1,3),(3,1,4)(n_{0},n_{1},n_{2})=(3,1,2),\;(3,1,3),\;(3,1,4), respectively. In fact, when (n0,n1,n2)=(3,2,2),(4,1,3),(6,1,2)(n_{0},n_{1},n_{2})=(3,2,2),\;(4,1,3),\;(6,1,2), it is also the Dynkin diagram of the affine Kac-Moody Lie algebra of types E6(1),E7(1),E8(1)E_{6}^{(1)},\;E_{7}^{(1)},\;E_{8}^{(1)}, respectively (cf. [Kv]). These diagrams are special examples of trees in graph theory.

A tree 𝒯{\cal T} consists of a finite set of nodes 𝒩={ι1,ι2,…,ιn}{\cal N}=\{\iota_{1},\iota_{2},...,\iota_{n}\} and a set of edges

ℰ⊂{(ιi,ιj)∣1≤i<j≤n}{\cal E}\subset\{(\iota_{i},\iota_{j})\mid 1\leq i<j\leq n\} (1.4)

such that for each node ιi∈𝒩\iota_{i}\in{\cal N}, there exists a unique sequence {ιi1,ιi2,…,ιir}\{\iota_{i_{1}},\iota_{i_{2}},...,\iota_{i_{r}}\} of nodes with 1=i1<i2<⋯<ir−1<ir=i1=i_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{r-1}<i_{r}=i for which

(ιi1,ιi2),(ιi2,ιi3),…,(ιir−2,ιir−1),(ιir−1,ιir)∈ℰ.(\iota_{i_{1}},\iota_{i_{2}}),(\iota_{i_{2}},\iota_{i_{3}}),...,(\iota_{i_{r-2}},\iota_{i_{r-1}}),(\iota_{i_{r-1}},\iota_{i_{r}})\in{\cal E}. (1.5)

We also denote the tree 𝒯=(𝒩,ℰ){\cal T}=({\cal N},{\cal E}). We identify a tree 𝒯=(𝒩,ℰ){\cal T}=({\cal N},{\cal E}) with a graph by depicting a small circle for each node in 𝒩{\cal N} and a segment connecting iith circle to jjth circle for the edge (ιi,ιj)∈ℰ(\iota_{i},\iota_{j})\in{\cal E} (cf. the above Dynkin diagrams of type AA and EE).

For a tree 𝒯=(𝒩,ℰ){\cal T}=({\cal N},{\cal E}), we call the differential operator

d𝒯=∂x12+∑(ιi,ιj)∈ℰxi∂xj2d_{\cal T}=\partial_{x_{1}}^{2}+\sum_{(\iota_{i},\iota_{j})\in{\cal E}}x_{i}\partial_{x_{j}}^{2} (1.6)

a generalized Tricomi operator of type 𝒯{\cal T}. Moreover, we call the partial differential equation

ut=d𝒯​(u)u_{t}=d_{\cal T}(u) (1.7)

a generalized heat conduction equation associated with the tree 𝒯{\cal T}, where uu is a function in t,x1,x2,…,xnt,x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n}. For instance, the generalized heat equation of type 𝒯En1,n2n0{\cal T}_{E^{n_{0}}_{n_{1},n_{2}}} is:

+xn0∂xn0+12+∑i=1n1−1xn0+2​i−1∂xn0+2​i+12)(u).(1.8)\displaystyle+x_{n_{0}}\partial_{x_{n_{0}+1}}^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{n_{1}-1}x_{n_{0}+2i-1}\partial_{x_{n_{0}+2i+1}}^{2})(u).\hskip 150.79968pt(1.8)

Let m1,m2,…,mnm_{1},m_{2},...,m_{n} be nn positive integers. The difficulty of solving the equation (1.7) is the same as that of solving the following more general evolution partial differential equation:

ut=(∂x1m1+∑(ιi,ιj)∈ℰxi∂xjmj)(u).u_{t}=(\partial_{x_{1}}^{m_{1}}+\sum_{(\iota_{i},\iota_{j})\in{\cal E}}x_{i}\partial_{x_{j}}^{m_{j}})(u). (1.9)

One of our main objectives is to solve the equation (1.9) subject to the initial condition:

u⁡(0,x1,…,xn)=f⁡(x1,…,xn)for​xi∈[−ai,ai],u(0,x_{1},...,x_{n})=f(x_{1},...,x_{n})\qquad\mbox{for}\;\;x_{i}\in[-a_{i},a_{i}], (1.10)

where ff is a given continuous function and aia_{i} are given positive real constants.

Our strategy of solving the above problem is first to attack simpler first-order evolution partial differential equations. Denote by ℤ+\mathbb{Z}_{+} the set of positive integers. We define a tree diagram 𝒯d{\cal T}^{d} to be a tree 𝒯=(𝒩,ℰ){\cal T}=({\cal N},{\cal E}) with a weight map d:ℰ→ℤ+d:{\cal E}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{+}, denoted as 𝒯d=(𝒩,ℰ,d){\cal T}^{d}=({\cal N},{\cal E},d). Moreover, we associate a tree diagram 𝒯d{\cal T}^{d} with a first-order partial differential equation:

ut=(∂x1+∑(ιi,ιj)∈ℰxid⁡[(ιi,ιj)]∂xj)(u).u_{t}=(\partial_{x_{1}}+\sum_{(\iota_{i},\iota_{j})\in{\cal E}}x_{i}^{d[(\iota_{i},\iota_{j})]}\partial_{x_{j}})(u). (1.11)

The above equation is a “dual” of (1.9) in a certain sense. It is also an equation of polynomial transformations for vector fields and may have practical applications. Our another objective is to solve (1.11) subject to the initial value condition:

u(0,x1,x2,….,xn)=f(x1,x2,…,xn)u(0,x_{1},x_{2},....,x_{n})=f(x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n}) (1.12)

for any given first-order differentiable function ff.

We remark that completely solving a linear partial differential equation with large number of variables is in general a difficult problem. The method of characteristic lines usually works only for linear partial differential equations with few variables. In order to solve (1.11), we have to use certain hidden symmetry.

Given a positive integer nn, we denote

𝔸=∑m1,m2,…,mn=0∞ℂ[x1,x2,…,xn]∂x1m1∂x2m2⋯∂xnmn,\mathbb{A}=\sum_{m_{1},m_{2},...,m_{n}=0}^{\infty}\mathbb{C}[x_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n}]\partial_{x_{1}}^{m_{1}}\partial_{x_{2}}^{m_{2}}\cdots\partial_{x_{n}}^{m_{n}}, (1.13)

[A,B]=A​B−B​Afor​A,B∈𝔸.[A,B]=AB-BA\qquad\mbox{for}\;\;A,B\in\mathbb{A}. (1.14)

In Section 2, we will completely determine the abelian ideals of the Lie algebra L1​(𝒯d)L_{1}({\cal T}^{d}). The abelian ideals of the Lie algebra ℒ1​(𝒯d){\cal L}_{1}({\cal T}^{d}) will be determined in Section 3. In Section 4, we will use some abelian ideals of L1​(𝒯d)L_{1}({\cal T}^{d}) and a high-order Campbell-Hausdorff formula to solve the equation (1.11) subject to the condition (1.12). In Section 5, we will use the results in Section 4 to solve the equation (1.9) subject to the condition (1.10).
